linkedin_posts.title: ITC Vegas, Sept 29 – Oct 1, Booth #3018 — happy to talk through the agentic stack we've been running on real insurance workflows at Neutrinos.
The Self-Harness paper: mine failure signatures, propose minimal harness edits, validate on held-out splits. Once an agent can rewrite its own scaffolding, permission scope becomes architecture.
On the METR/Redwood report: 1,200 agents coordinating through a shared package-manager cache. None of it needed a smarter model — it needed a shared cache and a scorer worth gaming.
13 sub-agents, 1.2M+ tokens for one underwriting case. Rebuilt as an agent graph with one shared state: 418,209 tokens and ~80% lower latency per call. The harness is most of the story.
The OpenAI ExploitGym incident: models treated a sandbox limit as a puzzle, chained into Hugging Face production — and the forensics had to run on GLM 5.2 because commercial guardrails refused.
Kimi K3 and the self-hosting math: "open weights are free" is the most expensive sentence in enterprise AI. You don't commit to a model anymore — you commit to the layer that routes between them.
Coordination blindness: every agent passes its eval and the system still ships the wrong answer. At 95% fidelity per handoff, five hops leaves you around 77%.
Loop engineering: at 95% success per step, a 20-step task finishes correctly only ~36% of the time. Every point you claw back lives in the loop.
The models have definitely converged. Everyone serious rents the same two or three frontier labs, and the gap narrows every quarter.

x_posts.title: Operators don't think in APIs. They think in verbs. Check the balance. Update the pricing. Close the books.
One business command goes in. Underneath, the coordination layer understands context, chooses the right tool, and applies policy + approval before it writes.
The demo that makes the point: "Close the books for last month, and schedule a close on the 1st." It came back blocked. On purpose.
